abstract: Thrombospondin-4 (THBS4) has long been catalogued as a pentameric extracellular matrix glycoprotein deposited in tendon and oxidative skeletal muscle, yet a growing body of loss-of-function, transcriptomic and cell-biological work now demands a reappraisal of this view. Ablation of Thbs4 in mice enlarges tendon collagen fibrils, reduces oxidative-muscle mass and grip strength, impairs local lipoprotein lipase activity and lipid uptake, and produces age-progressive dystrophic changes that can be rescued by overexpression in mouse and Drosophila models. At the molecular level, THBS4 stabilises the sarcolemma by promoting vesicular trafficking of dystrophin–glycoprotein and integrin attachment complexes, while in cardiomyocytes its type-3 repeat and C-terminal TSP-C domains engage the endoplasmic-reticulum chaperone BiP and the unfolded-protein-response sensor ATF6α, driving an adaptive secretory programme. These findings reframe THBS4 as an active organiser of muscle membrane and matrix homeostasis rather than a passive scaffold. Human exercise biology adds a further twist: eccentric running induces THBS4 as a hub gene within a secretome-enriched muscle co-expression module, raising—but not yet proving—the possibility that THBS4 acts as an exercise-responsive myokine. Quantitative plasma kinetics, receptor identification on distant targets and human confirmation of the chaperone-like programme in skeletal muscle all remain outstanding. Here I synthesise the mechanistic, metabolic and ageing-related dimensions of THBS4 in skeletal muscle, critically assess whether the available evidence supports a bona fide myokine classification, and outline the experiments required to resolve this question.
